This defence for Black can transpose into the Caro-Cann defence after '''2. e4 d5''' or '''2. d4 d5 3. e4'''.
Also it can transpose into Rapport-Jobava after '''2. d4 d5 3. Bf4'''.
If you don't want to transpose into these openings, you can play '''2. b3!?''' to prepare for fiachettoing to the bishop. '''2... d5 3. e3 e5 4.Bb2''' is giving Black centre, but fianchettoing the bishop.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Zukertort Opening |moves=1. Nf3 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A04-A09]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] }} == 1. Nf3 · Zukertort opening == '''1. Nf3''' is the third most popular initial move. It is highly flexible and often transposes into lines better known through other move orders, though some independent lines are possible. White reckons that Nf3 will almost certainly be a useful move sooner or later, whereas every pawn move is an irrevocable commitment, so 1. Nf3 keeps White's options open. This means it is a useful transpositional tool. White can feel out how Black wishes to play then transpose into their preferred line. For example, a player who hates facing the queen's gambit declined, but doesn't mind the Dutch defence might play 1. Nf3 and only follow with 2. d4 if Black plays [[/1...f5|'''1...f5''']]. Because 1. Nf3 controls the e5 square, [[/1...e5|'''1...e5?''']] would be quite bad. Therefore White can use this move order to avoid certain continuations with ...e5: if they wish to play the classical Nimzo-Larsen attack (1. b3 d5) but avoid the modern line (1. b3 e5); or a symmetrical English (1. c4 c5) but not a reversed Sicilian (1. c4 e5); they may choose to start with 1. Nf3. Black's main way to play is to deny White 2. e4 with either '''1...Nf6''' or '''1...d5'''. This leads to a number of transpositions and some more independent lines. [[/1...d5|'''1...d5''']] takes space in the centre and prevents White from playing 2. e4?. The main replies are: * 2. d4, which often leads to the Colle system or the queen's gambit by transposition; * 2. g3, the king's Indian attack, otherwise seen in the French defence; * 2. c4, the Réti, one of the most "independent" lines after 1. Nf3; * 2. b3, the classical variation of the Nimzo-Larsen. * 2. d3, with the idea of Nbd2 and e4, the old Indian attack. * If 2. e4? is played anyway, this is the Tennison gambit, otherwise reached from the Scandinavian defence 1. e4 d5 2. Nf3?. [[/1...Nf6|'''1...Nf6''']] is the most common reply in high-level chess. Black ''also'' avoids making a committing pawn move. Chief replies are: * 2. d4, often transposing either to an Indian defence or to a 1. d4 d5 opening. * 2. c4, transposing into the English opening, * 2. g3, again with the idea of Bg2 and the king's Indian attack. [[/1...c5|'''1...c5''']] looks to prevent 2. d4 instead. This invites White to transpose into the Sicilian defence with 2. e4, or the symmetrical English with 2. c4. [[/1...e5|'''1...e5?''']] has a name, the '''Ross gambit''', but just loses a pawn immediately. If played anyway, it's sometimes with the idea of 2. Nxe5 Nc6?! 3. Nxc6 dxc6, called (for whatever reason) the Walrus. [[/1...Nc6|'''1...Nc6''']], called the '''black mustang defence''', invites White to transpose to normality with 2. e4 e5. However, it doesn't prevent 2. d4 because the d4 square will immediately be protected by White's queen. '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...g6|1...g6]]''' is the '''Kingside Fianchetto'''. Black decides to fianchetto their kingside bishop on g7, which has ideas of transposing into a Modern Defence after 2. e4 Bg7 3. d4, or White can copy with 2. g3. '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...e6|1...e6]]''' is the '''Queen's Gambit Invitation'''. If 2. d4 or 2. c4 is played, it could transpose to a Queen's Gambit Declined. 2. e4 transposes to the Knight Variation of the French Defence. '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...d6|1...d6]]''' is the '''Pirc Invitation''' which may transpose into a 2. Nf3 Pirc Defence after 2. e4 or an Indian Defence after 2. d4 Nf6. A unique option after 2. d4 is 2...e5?, the dubious '''Vos Gambit'''. '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...c6|1...c6]]''' is the '''Slav Invitation'''. Although more passive than other responses to 1. Nf3, this is nonetheless playable and relatively good and can transpose into a Slav after 2. d4 d5 3. c4. Rarer moves include: * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...b6|1...b6]]''', the '''Queenside Fianchetto Variation''' trying to fianchetto on b7. * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...f6|1...f6?]]''', the '''Arctic Defence''', preparing e5, although 1...d6 is a better way of doing so. * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...a6|1...a6?!]]''', the '''St. George Defence''', playing in the style of the St. George that is 1. e4 a6. * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...a5|1...a5?!]]''', the '''Ware Defence''', does nothing to help Black's position. * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...h6|1...h6?!]]''', the '''Basman Defence''', prepares g5. * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...g5|1...g5?]]''', the '''Herrstrom Gambit''', an unsound gambit with the idea of kicking the knight around after 2. Nxg5 e5. * '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...b5|1...b5?!]]''', the '''Polish Defence''', playing a Polish/Orangutan Opening with colors reversed. === History === When Indian chess master [[Wikipedia:Moheschunder Bannerjee|Moheschunder Bannerjee]]'s games with [[Wikipedia:John Cochrane (chess player)|John Cochrane]] were published in the 1850s in Britain, they introduced ideas on flank and fianchetto openings from Indian chess (such as the "Indian defence") to European chess, and included the earliest games with 1. Nf3.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessplayer?pid=85637 Moheschunder Bannerjee - Chessgames.com] [[w:Johannes Zukertort|Johannes Zukertort]] (1842―1888) was a master chess player, known for competing against [[w:Wilhelm Steinitz|Wilhelm Steinitz]] in 1886 in what is considered to be the first "official" World Chess Championship. He employed 1. Nf3 in some of his games in his 1880 match against [[w:Samuel Rosenthal|Samuel Rosenthal]][https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1255757 Zukertort v Rosenthal, 1880. Chessgames.com][https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1255761 Zukertort v Rosenthal, 1880. Chesssgames.com][https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1255761 Zukertort v Rosenthal, 1880. Chesssgames.com] and used it intermittently from then on. Depending on who you ask, 1. Nf3 is the Zukertort and the continuation 1...d5 2. c4 is the Réti, for [[w:Richard Réti|Richard Réti]], or 1. Nf3 is the '''Réti''' and 1. Nf3 d5 2. c4 is the '''Réti gambit'''. == Theory table == {{ChessTable}} '''1. Nf3'''

= Zukertort Opening: Ross Gambit =

=== 1...e5? ===
The move 1...e5? by black, also known as the '''Ross Gambit''', is a dubious pawn sacrifice for black to try and kick the knight as much as possible and potentially even trap it if white's not careful. This gambit can be accepted by playing the move '''[[/2._Nxe5|2. Nxe5]]''', however white can also decline the gambit with '''[[/2._e4|2. e4]]''' transposing to the King's Knight Opening, '''[[/2._d3|2. d3]]''' stopping ...e4, or '''[[/2._d4|2. d4]]''' attacking the pawn on e5, however allowing ...e4.

= Dutch Defence =
===1...f5===
Black's opening move aims to transpose into a Dutch Defence. [[/2. d4|2.d4]] gives a main-line Dutch, while [[/2. c4|2.c4]] and [[/2. g3|2.g3]] reserve options.

A major independent option is [[/2. e4|2.e4]]. The sacrifice of White's e-pawn is borrowed from the [[../../1. d4/1...f5/2. e4|Staunton Gambit]], but the positional themes are very different since here White's king's knight can reach g5.

[[/2. d3|2.d3]] is a way of preparing e4.

Nh3 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A00]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] }} == 1. Nh3?! · Ammonia Opening == The Ammonia opening is based on the chemical formula of ammonia (NH3) and the fact that ammonia, like this opening, 'stinks'. Other titles for this opening include the Amar Opening, the Paris Opening, and Drunken Knight Opening. Chess author Tim Harding has jokingly suggested that "Amar" is an acronym for "Absolutely mad and ridiculous"; that sums up this move! Jokes aside, this move isn’t actually bad, it just does not improve White's position. White has made an odd decision to develop the knight to a square where it has very little influence on the game (knights generally hate the edge of the board, and love the centre). As such, Black can fairly easily get an edge. === Black's responses === White’s choice has effectively surrendered the first move to Black. Any one of White's opening moves may be employed by Black (except, of course, 1... g5??, which loses a pawn ''and'' weakens the kingside). * [[/1...e5|'''1... e5''']] * [[/1...d5|'''1... d5''']] == All possible Black's moves == {| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="10" | style="text-align:left; vertical-align:top;"|'''Quick'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Ware Opening |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A00]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] }} == 1. a4?! · Ware opening == '''1. a4?!''' is an unorthodox opening. It does not help White to develop their pieces or stake a claim to the centre. It is almost like White has passed their first turn: functionally, they are playing a tempo down. It is most common with beginners who think that their rooks are powerful pieces, and wouldn't it be good to develop them first? Unfortunately, rook lifting (a4, Ra3, Rd3 etc) is too slow and gives Black plenty of time to develop all their minor pieces. Rooks come alive later in the game, when files begin to open. After 1. a4, Black gets to decide which pawn to put in the centre. [[/1...e5|'''1...e5''']] is the main line (as much as there is a "main line"), taking space and opening the a3-f8 diagonal for Black's bishop. As long as White responds with something like 2. e4 then they do not fall too far behind and the game is even. A classic beginner blunder (called sometimes the '''meadow hay trap''') marries the plan of an early rook lift with a lack of board vision: 2. Ra3?? Bxa3. [[/1...d5|'''1...d5''']] is also very sound. [[/1...a5|'''1...a5?!''']], which might be called the "symmetrical variation", at worst fails to capitalise on White's irregular play. === History === 1. a4 is named for [[w:Preston Ware|Preston Ware]] who played it in 1880 during the 5th American Chess Congress.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1255664 Ware v Congdon, 1880. Chessgames.com][https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1255734 Ware v Delmar, 1880. Chessgames.com] With the black pieces he played 1...a5.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1255680 Mackenzie v Ware, 1880. Chessgames.com] Contemporaries of Ware called 1. a4 the '''meadow hay opening'''.{{Cite journal |title=The fifth American chess congress and its international tourney. |journal=The American Chess Journal |date=1880-04-01 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.hn43v8 |volume=1 |issue=3}} [[w:Magnus Carlsen|Magnus Carlsen]] played it against [[w:Teimour Radjabov|Teimour Radjabov]] in the 2012 World Blitz Championship, apparently as an in-joke referencing Radjabov's comment, "Everyone is getting tired. You might as well start with 1. a4 and you can still beat them."[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1671724 Carlsen v Radjabov, 2012. Chessgames.com]{{cite news|url=http://www.chessvibes.com/reports/grischuk-wins-2nd-world-blitz-title-in-astana|publisher=ChessVibes|title=Grischuk wins 2nd World Blitz title in Astana|date=10 July 2012|access-date=11 July 2012|archive-date=12 July 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120712124143/http://www.chessvibes.com/reports/grischuk-wins-2nd-world-blitz-title-in-astana|url-status=dead}} In May 2024, the opening gained notoriety after Grandmaster [[w:Brandon Jacobson|Brandon Jacobson]], under the pseudonym Viih_Sou, won a sixty-nine game blitz match against [[w:Daniel Naroditsky|Daniel Naroditsky]] by playing 1. a4 and 2. Ra3? with White and 1...a5 & 2...Ra6? with Black every game, voluntarily sacrificing the exchange. Chess.com banned Viih_Sou for fair play violations and the line became known as the "banned gambit" or "Viih_Sou gambit". Jacobson took to [[w:Reddit|Reddit]] to reveal their identity and deny allegations of cheating.{{Cite web |title=An offer you can't refuse... |url=https://en.chessbase.com/post/an-offer-you-can-t-refuse |last=Ris |first=Robert |date=2024-05-05 |website=ChessBase}}[https://www.reddit.com/r/chess/comments/1claxsm/its_me_viih_sou/ ''It's me. Viih_Sou.''] Brandon Jacobson, Reddit.com/r/chess. Brandon Jacobson went on to win with 1. a4 (though not 2. Ra3?) against [[w:Hikaru Nakamura|Hikaru Nakamura]] in the 2024 World Rapid Championship.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2817219 Jacobson v Nakamura, 2024. pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Nimzowitsch–Larsen attack |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A01]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] }} == 1. b3 · Nimzowitsch–Larsen attack == '''1. b3''' prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop to b2, where it will fight for the central squares and point towards Black's kingside. This is a [[Wikipedia:Hypermodernism (chess)|hypermodern opening]], preparing to control the centre from afar with a bishop rather than a central pawn (the classical style). This allows Black to seize the centre with a pawn themselves, which they usually choose to do with either 1...e5 or 1...d5. 1...Nf6 is also common. [[/1...e5|'''1...e5''']], the '''modern variation''', is Black's most ambitious and common response to 1. b3, occurring in about 45% of games. Black usually limits the scope of White's bishop and gets a big centre with both d and e pawns after 2. Bb2 Nc6 3. e3 d5. [[/1...d5|'''1...d5''']], the '''classical variation''', is a common sideline (27%). It preserves the option to fianchetto the black bishop to g7 to oppose the white one. White can play 2. Bb2 or 2. Nf3. [[/1...Nf6|'''1...Nf6''']], the '''Indian variation''', prepares to fianchetto the bishop to g7 immediately to oppose the white bishop on b2. However, if Black does play g6 after 2. Bb2, White can play 3. e4!, threatening to kick the knight on f6. 3...Nxe4?? loses to 4. Bxh8. It is an interesting second sideline (15%). ===Minor sidelines=== * [[/1...c5|'''1...c5''']], '''English variation''': Retains option of 1...d5 while also being a good transpositional tool. 2. e4 transposes into the Sicilian defence, and 2. c4 transposes into the symmetrical English. 2. Nf3 is also playable. Occurs about 5% of games. * '''1...b6''', '''Symmetrical variation''': Black copies White's idea. This is perfectly fine for Black. Occurs about 2% of games. * '''1...g6''': Accounts for another 2% of games. Black prepares to fianchetto to g7, though after 2. Bb2 Black must play 2...Nf6 first and this transposes to the Indian variation. There are a number of other "also-ran" sidelines possible that together make up about 5% of competitive level games, including: * '''1...f5''', '''Dutch variation''': This is a rather unexplored alternative. 2. d4 and 2. Nf3 are most commonly played after this, though 2. e3 and even 2. e4!? (borrowing ideas from the Staunton gambit) are both possible. * '''1...e6''': Sets up a variation of the French defence. 2. e4 d5 3. Bb2 is the most common and recommended line. * '''1...c6''': Sets up a variation of the Caro-Kann. 2. e4 d5 3. Bb2 is the most common and recommended line. * '''1...Nc6''': Supports the advance of the e-pawn but allows 2. d4, pressuring the knight. * '''1...b5!?''', '''Polish variation''': A fun alternative to the other moves. Transpositions are now impossible. * '''1...a5?!''': Somewhat playable, trying to ruin White's fianchetto, but seeing that White will likely castle on the kingside, this is not that useful. === History === Also known as '''Nimzowitsch-Larsen attack''' or just '''queen's fianchetto opening''', it is named after its pioneers [[w:Aron Nimzowitsch|Aron Nimzowitsch]] and [[w:Bent Larsen|Bent Larsen]]. Nimzowitsch preferred an alternate move order, [[../1. Nf3|1. Nf3]], and only after 1...d5 committing to 2. b3. This has the advantage of preventing 1...e5 thereby avoiding that line. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1.b3''' {| border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" |- ! ! align="left" | 1 ! align="left" | 2 ! align="left" | 3 ! align="left" | 4 ! align="left" | 5 ! align="left" | 6 ! align="left" | 7 ! align="left" | 8 |- ! align="right" | Classical Variation | ...

White normally completes the fianchetto through 2. Bb2, and black sets up the same pattern by attempting 2...g6 (where the knight shields the pawn.) White may then send out the kings knight with 3.Nf3, or claim the center with 3.e4 (with the knight being pinned). Less common is 2.Nf3, which lets black setup a fianchetto of his own. === Statistics === FICS Games Database shows the most common responses for white are Bb2 (64%), Nf3 (23%) and e3 (8%). ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}.

Having committed to b3 already, White's continuation is invariably '''2. Bb2''', but, since 1...c5 does not control e4 or c4, Black invites White to later play e4 themselves, transposing into a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. b3|b3 Sicillian]], or c4, transposing into a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...c5|Symmetrical English]], which Black hopes to be more comfortable playing. Most commonly, White declines this invitation and keeps things in Nimzo-Larsen territory with '''3. e3'''. Then, Black can choose to play e5 or d5 with the additional central control afforded by having already played c5. ==Theory table== '''1.b3 c5''' {| border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" |- ! ! align="left" | 2 ! align="left" | 3 ! align="left" | 4 ! align="left" | 5 ! align="left" | 6 ! align="left" | 7 ! align="left" | 8 ! align="left" | 9 |- ! align="right" | Nimzowitsch-Larsen Attack,

Chess Opening Theory/1. b3/1...e5
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Modern variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A01]] |parent=[[../|Nimzowitsch-Larsen attack]] }} ==1...e5 · Modern variation== By beginning with '''1. b3''', White allowed Black to take the centre with '''1...e5'''. This is the most popular and ambitious continuation for Black. Some are dismissive of the 1. b3 move order because of this reply: White is left playing an [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6|Owen's Defence]] with colours reversed, "and not even an extra tempo can make that fully respectable."{{cite book |last=Schiller |first1=Eric |date=1998 |title=Unorthodox Chess Openings |location=New York |publisher=Cardoza Publishing |isbn=0 940685 73 6 |edition=1st |pp=304-306}} For this reason, Nimzowitsch preferred[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1051397 Nimzowitsch opening collection, chessgames.com] the move order 1. Nf3 (preventing e5) d5 2. b3. On the other hand, by not playing Nf3 yet, White retains the option of f4 to contest e5 later. Having already prepared to fianchetto with 1. b3, White's continuation is invariably '''2. Bb2'''. '''2...Nc6''', to defend the e5 pawn, follows, though the timid '''2...d6''' is occasionally tried. White may then play '''3. c4''' to prevent 3...d5, but normally, White is happy to allow Black to take over the centre with both e5 and d5, planning to later attack it with the flank c and f pawns. Instead, the typical Nimzo-Larsen plan is to continue with the more patient '''3. e3''', opening up their other bishop.{{cite book |last1=Jacobs |first1=Byron |last2=Tait |first2=Jonathan |date=2001 |title=Nimzo-Larsen attack |location=London |publisher=Everyman Publishers plc |isbn=1 85744 286 5 |edition=1st}} ==Theory table== '''1.b3 e5''' {| border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" |- ! ! align="left" | 2 ! align="left" | 3 ! align="left" | 4 ! align="left" | 5 ! align="left" | 6 ! align="left" | 7 ! align="left" | 8 ! align="left" | 9 |- ! align="right" | Nimzowitsch-Larsen Attack,

__NOTOC__ {{Chess Opening Theory/Position|Polish Opening| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd|nd|rd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |pl| | | | | | | | | | | | | | |pl| |pl|pl|pl|pl|pl|pl|rl|nl|bl|ql|kl|bl|nl|rl|eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A00]] |moves=1. b4 |parent=[[../|Starting position]] |responses=
* [[/1...e5|1...e5 - Main Line]] * [[/1...d5|1...d5]] * [[/1...Nf6|1...Nf6]] * [[/1...f5|1...f5 - Dutch Defence]] * [[/1...c6|1...c6 - Outflank Variation]] * [[/1...b5 |1...b5 - Symmetrical Variation]] * [[/1...c5 |1...c5 - Birmingham Gambit]] * [[/1...Nc6|1...Nc6 - Grigorian Variation]] * [[/1...Nh6|1...Nh6 - Karniewski Variation]]}} == 1. b4 · Polish Opening == The Polish Opening (or Orangutan Opening) is a flank and rather uncommon opening starting with the move 1. b4. The purpose of this move is to fight for a spatial advantage on the queenside instead of immediately taking control of the centre. White will claim their share of the centre after getting the queen’s bishop fianchettoed and an eventual pawn advance in the centre. The move b4 can always be played later in the game which is the reason why this opening is seldom seen nowadays, however, Tartakower and Magnus Carlsen have tried it in tournaments and won successfully. The Polish opening is classified under the code (A00) as an irregular opening. * Fianchettoing is often a good idea. Why not grab a little space? * At some point a quick b4-b5 might dislodge a knight on c6. * Trading the b-pawn for the c-pawn may give white central power. * If Black responds with 1...e5 or 1...e6, usual play either continues with 2. a3, defending the pawn, or 2. Bb2, fianchettoing the bishop on the powerful a1-h8 diagonal. The idea after Bb2 is that the black can't play Bxb4 right away. For example, after 1. b4 e6 2. Bb2 Bxb4??, White responds with 3. Bxg7, at which point Black loses a rook. However, 1. b4 e5 2. Bb2 Bxb4!? 3. Bxe5 is actually viable for Black, in spite of the fact that Black cedes White a central pawn majority. Black will usually obtain some form of compensation with a slight lead in development. Chances for both sides in these lines are around equal, with perhaps a very slight edge for White. * Another possibility is for White to advance their b-pawn with b5, so as to evade attack. This has been shown to be a good option in several lines, and White now has a clear spatial advantage on the queenside. On the other hand, White’s pawn is now overextended and difficult to protect. Once again, the positions resulting from these lines are generally equal. == Theory table == '''1. b4'''

pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. c4
pages.wikitext:
__NOTOC__ {{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |English Opening| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd|nd|rd|= |pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|= | | | | | | | | |= | | | | | | | | |= | | |pl| | | | | |= | | | | | | | | |= |pl|pl| |pl|pl|pl|pl|pl|= |rl|nl|bl|ql|kl|bl|nl|rl|= |moves= 1. c4 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A10-A39]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] }} == 1. c4 · English Opening == '''1. c4''' is the '''English Opening'''. It is the fourth most commonly played opening move in chess. By playing this move, White allows the queen to move freely and also discourages Black from responding with 1...d5. Additionally, White ensures that the c-pawn will not be blocked behind a knight on c3. The resulting positions often resemble those that arise from 1. d4 openings rather than 1. e4 openings, and the move d4 is frequently played later on. While this opening is not as sharp as 1. e4 or 1. d4, it is still effective in controlling the d5 square and is highly flexible, allowing for easy transpositions into other openings, and is often used when White desires to avoid certain responses to 1. d4 by Black. For example, transposition to [[Chess/Queen's Gambit|Queen's Gambit]] and [[Chess/Indian Defence|Indian Defence]] positions are very frequently seen. === Black's responses === * [[/1...Nf6/]] is likely to transpose into an [[Chess/Indian Defence|Indian Defence]] or one of the alternative lines below. * [[/1...e5/]] is a reversed [[Chess/Sicilian Defence|Sicilian Defence]], but the extra tempo for White changes the patterns noticeably. * [[/1...e6/]] prepares 2...d5 and is known as the Agincourt Defense. It often ends up transposing to a [[Chess/Queen's Gambit|Queen's Gambit Declined]] or [[Chess/Indian Defence|Indian Defence]]. An independent alternative line is the Mikėnas-Carls Variation, continuing 2. Nc3 Nf6 3. e4. * [[/1...c5/]] is the Symmetrical Variation, which has many unique lines. Often a d4 or d5 pawn break will occur later in the game. * [[/1...c6/]] will usually either transpose into the [[Chess/Caro-Kann Defence|Caro-Kann Defence]] or the [[Chess/Slav Defence|Slav Defence]]. * [[/1...f5/]], the Anglo-Dutch Defence, leads to sharp tactical lines for Black, but can open a powerful kingside attack. This is likely to transpose into the regular [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...f5|Dutch Defense]] after 2.d4. * [[/1...g6/]] is likely to transpose into a [[Chess/King's Indian Defence|King's Indian Defence]], Reversed Sicilian, or Symmetrical Variation. * [[/1...b6/]] will in all likelihood transpose into the [[Chess/English Defence|English Defence]]. * [[/1...d5/]] is seldom played but may transpose into the [[Chess/Queen's Gambit|Queen's Gambit]] or the [[Chess/Réti Opening|Réti Opening]]. * [[/1...b5/]], the Jaenisch or Halibut Gambit, can give good practical chances for Black, but is considered unsound at the professional level. * [[/1...g5/]], the Myers Defence, gives White a small advantage. * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...Nc6|1...Nc6]], the Anglo-Lithuanian Variation, is relatively rare, with 2. Nc3 or 2. g3 staying in the realm of English openings and 2. d4 transposing into a line in the Mikenas Defence. == Statistics == {| class="wikitable" |- ! move !! average !! 365Chess.com (big) !! = English Opening =
{{Chess/sideline}}
=== 1...Na6?! ===
Instead of developing conventionally with 1...Nc6 or 1...Nf6, Black develops their queenside knight to the rim instead of contesting the center and plays in similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Na6|Lemming Defence]]. This response to 1. c4 is rare and considered dubious.

White can choose from a variety of moves, such as:

* 2. d4, pushing a central pawn
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. g3, preparing to fianchetto the f1 bishop
* 2. b3, preparing to fianchetto the c1 bishop

= English Opening, Anglo-Lithuanian Variation =
With the Anglo-Lithuanian Variation, Black develops their queenside knight and aims to control the central squares. This is a relatively rare move in the English Opening and could be transpositional.

'''2. d4''' transposes into a line in the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nc6|Mikenas Defence]] (1. d4 Nc6 2. c4) and grabs space in the center. This is the most accurate move.

However, White can stay in the realm of English openings by playing '''2. Nc3''' or '''2. g3'''. This is the most popular approach.

= English Opening =
{{Chess/sideline}}
=== 1...Nh6?! ===
The rarest response to the English Opening in amateur play, playing in similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nh6|Adams/Hippopotamus Defence]]. Instead of contesting the center or developing the knight to f6, Black moves the knight to the rim for not much reason.

White can choose from a variety of responses, such as:

* 2. d4, pushing a central pawn to take control of the center
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight normally
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight normally
* 2. g3, preparing to fianchetto the kingside bishop.
* 2. b3, preparing to fianchetto the queenside bishop.

= English Opening =

=== 1...a5 ===
Instead of developing a piece or contesting the center, Black plays in similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...a5|Ware Defence]]. This move is a rare response to 1. c4 and hasn't been seen much. Black may want to develop their rook to a6 or march their a-pawn down the board to ruin White's queenside.

White can choose from a variety of responses, such as:

* 2. d4, pushing a central pawn to take the center for free
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. g3, preparing to fianchetto the f1 bishop
* 2. b3, preparing to fianchetto the c1 bishop

=== 1...a6!? ===
A very interesting move by black. The idea is to play b5 and chip away White's strong c4 pawn. If white tries to stop it with '''[[/2. Nc3|2. Nc3]]''', black can play a gambit with 2...b5!?, pushing anyways, with the point of when white accepts it with 3. cxb5 axb5 4. Nxb5, white has 4...e5 or 4...d5, taking the entire center and preparing potential plans of a queenside attack.

Play varies greatly depending on how White chooses to develop. For instance, 2. Nf3 signals that White will try to achieve a favourable break with the d-pawn immediately and Black can then try to impede this break and achieve his own immediate d-pawn break. 2. Nc3 on the other hand makes it harder for Black to achieve that pawn break and signals White's intention to develop first and then break the symmetry. For instance, common moves for White in this variation include g3, Bg2, e4, Nge2, d3, and O-O (the arising white pawn structure is called the Botvinnik system) with the idea of a pawn break on f4, b4, or even d4. White may also play e3 instead of e4 and once the knight gets to e2 the pawn break on d4 becomes a very attractive possibility. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}

= English Opening =

=== 1...f6?! ===
A rare and less conventional response to the English Opening. Black plays in similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...f6|Barnes Defence]], weakening the king and stripping the kingside knight of its most natural developing square, though not quite as weak as 1. e4 f6 or 1. d4 f6 as White doesn't have an immediate way of exploiting the weakness and prepares e5 without any tactical pitfalls (e.g. 1. e4 f6? 2. d4 e5 3. dxe5 fxe5?? 4. Qh5+!).

White can choose from a variety of responses, such as:

* 2. d4, taking part of the center for free
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. g3, preparing to fianchetto the f1 bishop
* 2. b3, preparing to fianchetto the c1 bishop

= Mieses Opening: Reversed Rat =

== 1...e5 ==
With 1...e5, named the '''Reversed Rat'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Mieses Opening: Reversed Rat |url=https://lichess.org/opening/Mieses_Opening_Reversed_Rat/d3_e5 |access-date=2026-04-14 |website=lichess.org |language=en-US}}</ref>, Black takes the center as White didn't so it themselves with their timid starting move. The Mieses Opening is usually flexible for White as they haven't made a big commitment yet.

=== Responses ===
The most common amateur move<ref name=":0" />, '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d3/1...e5/2. e4|2. e4]]''', transposes to the Leonardis Variation of the King's Pawn Opening<ref>{{Cite web |title=King's Pawn Game: Leonardis Variation |url=https://lichess.org/opening/Kings_Pawn_Game_Leonardis_Variation/d3_e5_e4 |access-date=2026-04-14 |website=lichess.org |language=en-US}}</ref>. Although it controls the center, it doesn't fully help White's development as their f1 bishop is blocked by the pawn on d3.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d3/1...e5/2. c4|2. c4]]''', Stockfish's most preferred move, transposes to a line more commonly seen in the English Opening (1. c4 e5 2. d3). It controls a central square, d5, and helps the b1 white knight to develop to c3 without blocking the c-pawn which would usually be on c2.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d3/1...e5/2. Nf3|2. Nf3]]''' is a good move, attacking the pawn on e5 while developing the knight on g1. Black cannot kick the knight away with 2...e4 as the pawn on d3 controls e4.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d3/1...e5/2. g3|2. g3]]''' has the simple idea of fianchettoing the kingside bishop to g2, as on the f1-a6 diagonal, the pawn on d3 blocks it from reaching anywhere past e2.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d3/1...e5/2. Nd2|2. Nd2]]''', the Valencia Opening<ref>{{Cite web |title=Valencia Opening |url=https://lichess.org/opening/Valencia_Opening/d3_e5_Nd2 |access-date=2026-04-14 |website=lichess.org |language=en-US}}</ref>, is a less orthodox response to 1...e5 as it blocks in the queenside bishop and cramps White's development a bit. However, it is fully playable as it develops the knight towards the center and the c1 bishop still has options of fianchettoing to b2 after the b-pawn moves to b3.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d3/1...e5/2. d4|2. d4!?]]''' reaches a position which is identical to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5|Scandinavian Defence]], but with colours reversed. Any position that can be reached from the normal Scandinavian can be reached from 2. d4!?, just with colours flipped.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Queen's Pawn opening |moves=1. d4 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A40-A99]], [[Chess/ECOD|D00-D99]] and [[Chess/ECOE|E00-E99]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] |responses=
* [[/1...d5|1...d5 · Closed game]] * [[/1...Nf6|1...Nf6 · Indian defence]] }} == 1. d4 · Queen's Pawn opening == '''1. d4''' is the '''Queen's pawn opening'''. With 1. d4 White looks to take over control of the centre. The pawn directly controls the c5 and e5 squares, and White's queen now 'sees' the d4 square. 1. d4 is also a developing move in that it opens a diagonal for the queen's bishop to venture into the game later. 1. d4 is the second most common first move, after 1. e4. As the d4 pawn is already supported by the queen, the opening moves of Queen's Pawn games tend to be less forcing than King's Pawn games. This leads, in general, to games that are more closed and positional than open and tactical. 1. d4 is aimed at slowing down Black's development rather than accelerating White's. If allowed, White could play 2. e4 next and achieve a big, two-pawn centre, and develop comfortably in all the space that affords them. Therefore a priority for Black is to prevent this. === Control e4 === The chief approach to preventing 2. e4 is to control the e4 square. [[/1...d5|'''1...d5''']], the '''Closed game''', is the classical approach. It controls the c4 and e4 squares, and so if White does play 2. e4, they at least cannot keep the pawn there. 1...d5 also prevents White from pushing their d4 pawn to d5, and so secures some space for Black to develop. Additionally, like 1. d4 for White, 1...d5 helps Black to develop by releasing their queenside bishop. The most common continuation is 2. c4, the Queen's gambit, the champagne and caviar of White openings. 1...d5 is the most common at the club level and the second most common reply in tournament games.26% of games in the Lichess Masters database continue 1...d5, and 45% of games in the Lichess database. [[/1...Nf6|'''1...Nf6''']], the '''Indian defence''', controls e4 while developing a knight. This is a more flexible response: Black may yet commit a pawn to the centre, like ...d5 to transpose into classical lines, or they may play in a hypermodern style where they control the centre from afar with their pieces. 1...Nf6 is the mainline today.61% of games in the Lichess Masters database continue 1...Nf6, and 21% of games in the Lichess database. [[/1...f5|'''1...f5''']], the '''Dutch defence''', controls e4 with a flank pawn. Black acts on the principle that trading an important central pawn for one of their more peripheral pawns would be good for them. Black can develop their g8 knight behind f pawn, and can create a robust pawn structure with e6 and d5 (the Stonewall set-up) or d6 and g6 (fianchettoing the bishop, the Leningrad). The Dutch is a minor sideline. Advancing one's f-pawn while one's king is still in the centre isn't for the faint of heart: an example trap that exploits the weak e8-to-h5 diagonal is: 2. e4 fxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 (to hold onto the pawn) 4. Bg5 d5?? 5. Bxf6 exf6 6. Qh5+ g6 7. Qxd5 Qxd5 8. Nxd5 (forking the f6 and c7 pawns). === Attack d4 === Another approach to preventing White from attaining the two-pawn centre is to attack d4. [[/1...e5|'''1...e5?!''']] is the '''Englund gambit'''. It offers White a pawn to deflect their pawn away from d4. This gambit is considered unsound, but it conceals many traps and has some success as a club-level line. If White prioritises their development over holding onto the pawn, they will enjoy a comfortable edge. [[/1...c5|'''1...c5''']] is the '''Old Benoni'''. It offers White a less valuable flank pawn for their central d4 pawn. If they accept it, Black can easily recover it and enjoy having two central pawns to White's one. However, White is not compelled to accept the pawn: the mainline is 2. d5. It results in closed positions where White has more space. === Allow 2. e4 === Alternatively, Black can allow White to play 2. e4 for now and look to undermine it later. Essentially Black gives White the option of transposing into an e4 opening (that Black hopes to be more familiar with than White). It's a curious fact that in practice White usually ''declines'' to play e4 right away even if allowed to do so, instead choosing to keep things in conventional Queen's pawn opening territory. [[/1...e6|'''1...e6''']], the '''Horwitz defence''', is the chief alternative to 1...d5 or 1...Nf6. This is essentially a transpositional trick: it invites White to play 2. e4 and [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5|transposes into the French defence]] after 2...d5, which happens about one in ten games. If Black plays the French against 1. e4, then this is a way to move to more familiar territory. If White chooses to stay in 1. d4 territory with 2. c4 instead, Black can transpose into a Queen's gambit declined (with 2...d5), a Dutch (2...f5), or a Nimzo-Indian/Bogo-Indian with 2...Nf6. Similar approaches offering transposition into an e4 opening include: * [[/1...c6|'''1...c6''']]: after 2. e4 d5, the game transposes to a Caro-Kann. Otherwise, White can play 2. c4 and the game becomes a Slav after 2...d5. * [[/1...Na6|'''1...Na6?!''']] is a vanishingly rare move that nonetheless has a name, the '''Australian defence''', which can transpose into the De Bruycker variation of the Caro-Kann after 2. e4 c6. * [[/1...Nc6|'''1...Nc6''']], the eccentric '''Mikenas defence''', invites 2. e4 and transposition into a Nimzowitsch defence, but 2. Nf3, 2. c4, or 2. d5 chasing the knight away are all more popular. * [[/1...b6|'''1...b6''']], the '''English defence''', prepares a queenside fianchetto. After 2. e4 it transposes to an Owen's defence, otherwise after 2. c4 Bb7 controls e4 and the game can have its own character where Black plays e6 and f5: 3. Nc3 e6 4. a3 f5 5. Nf3 Nf6. * [[/1...d6|'''1...d6''']] offering transposition into a '''Pirc defence''' after 2. e4, or if 2. c4 Black has prepared 2...e5, known as the '''Rat defence'''. * [[/1...g6|'''1...g6''']], preparing a kingside fianchetto and offers to transpose into a '''Modern defence'''. An outlier is [[/1...b5|'''1...b5!?''']], the '''Polish defence'''. Black both allows White to play 2. e4 ''and'' discourages 2. c4, therefore White is doubly encouraged to follow with 2. e4 and it is the main move. After 2. e4 Bb7, the trade of pawns 3. Bxb5 Bxe4 is the Spassky gambit. More common is 3. Bd3 to defend the pawn. === Wild gambits === It is not so easy to lose a pawn on the first move of the game, but it is possible. The Benoni, 1...c5, (see above) offers a pawn but if taken it can easily be recovered. The Englund gambit 1...e5?! (above) is also unsound, but affords Black practical chances at club level.Per the Lichess database, Black's success rate with 1...e5 is 47%, compared with 44% for the conventional 1...d5. If Black is determined to lose a pawn then the third option is 1...g5??. [[/1...g5|'''1...g5??''']] is the '''Borg gambit'''. Black gives up a pawn immediately (2. Bxg5). If Black is careless this can lead to a very quick checkmate (2...f6? 3. e4 fxg5?? 4. Qh5#). Otherwise, play continues 2...Bg7 3. e6 and Black's "plan" is to break on c5 quickly and hope to exploit White's queenside, which can no longer be defended by White's bishop. As an example: 3...c5 4. c3 (if 4. dxc5? Bxb2!) cxd4 5. cxd4?? Qa5+! 6. Nc3 Qxg5. == Theory table == {{ChessTable}} {{Chess/theory table |line1=1...Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Mikenas defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A40]] |parent=[[../|Queen's pawn opening]] |aka=Bogoljubov–Mikenas defence, Lundin defence, Nimzowitsch queen's pawn}} ==1...Nc6 · Mikenas defence == A rare move. 1...Nc6 develops a knight and prepares ...e5. Part of the idea is, like a reflection of the Alekhine defence, 1. e4 Nf6, to encourage White to overextend in the centre before counter-attacking. Original positions can arise if White plays d5, kicking the knight, either immediately, [[/2. d5|'''2. d5''']], or after a sequence like [[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']] e5 3. d5. Otherwise the often game transposes into positions more commonly reached by other move orders. [[/2. Nf3|'''2. Nf3''']] is most common move, developing and controlling e5. This allows Black to play 2...d5 and the game resumes some sense of normality, although it is unusual in 1. d4 d5 games for Black to play Nc6 so early and deprive themselves of the option to move their c-pawn. [[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']] d5 transposes into the Chigorin defence to the Queen's gambit, normally seen in the order 1. d4 d5 2. c4 Nc6. [[/2. e4|'''2. e4''']] transposes into the Nimzowitsch defence, usually seen after 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1.d4 Nc6'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Indian defence |parent=[[../|Queen's pawn opening]] |responses=
*[[/2. c4|2. c4]] *[[/2. Nf3|2. Nf3 · Knights variation]] *[[/2. Bg5|2. Bg5 · Trompowsky attack]] *[[/2. Bf4|2. Bf4 · Accelerated London/Indian]] }} == 1...Nf6 · Indian defence == Black controls e4 while developing a knight. This is the most flexible response to 1. d4. Black doesn't commit a pawn to the centre yet. They may yet do so, or they can fight for the centre in the hypermodern way: controlling it from afar with pieces, allowing White to construct their pawn centre but undermining it later with timely pawn advances. This move gives White lots of leeway to either develop pieces or take more space in the centre. Openings tend to be flexible with lots of potential for transpositions. === Take space in the centre === White would like two pawns in the centre if possible. [[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']] is the '''main line''': White takes more space and controls the important d5 square. After 2. c4, White can develop their knight behind their pawn line and perhaps play e4. Black can still choose to contest this centre with pawns with 2...d5, 2...c5 (Benoni), or 2...e5 (Budapest), but more typically they move their pawns only as necessary to develop their bishops: 2...e6, 2...g6, 2...d6 or 2...b6. White can't play e4 and keep the pawn there ([[/2. e4|'''2. e4?!''']] is called the '''Omega gambit''' and loses a pawn to 2...Nxe4). White can prepare 3. e4 with [[/2. Nc3|'''2. Nc3''']] or [[/2. f3|'''2. f3''']], which usually compels Black to play 2...d5 to keep control of e4. === Develop a piece === Alternatively, White can prioritise piece development. [[/2. Nf3|'''2. Nf3''']], the '''Knights variation''' is the chief sideline. It's a flexible move: White may still play c4 afterwards but first gets more information on how Black intends to play. [[/2. Nc3|'''2. Nc3''']], prevents c4 but, as noted above, prepares e4. After 2...d5 (controlling e4) the main continuations are 3. Bg5, the '''Richter-Veresov attack''', or 3. Bf4, the '''Jobava-Rapport London'''. The bishop has two main candidate squares to develop to. [[/2. Bg5|'''2. Bg5''']], the '''Trompowsky attack''', pressures Black's knight. White has hopes of trading it to double Black's pawns. [[/2. Bf4|'''2. Bf4''']] plays the '''Accelerated London system''' into Black's Indian defence. Play may [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Bf4/2...d5|transpose with 2...d5]], but the Indian defence has original ways to meet it without ...d5. === Uncommon moves === *[[/2. e3|'''2. e3''']] plays in [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. e3|'''Colle system''']]-style against the Indian defence. Transposes if Black plays ...d5. *[[/2. g3|'''2. g3''']], the '''Tartakower attack''', prepares to fianchetto the bishop. === Strange moves=== *[[/2. d5 |'''2. d5?!''']], the '''Pawn push variation'''. Since Black didn't play d5, White can advance their pawn, guarded by their queen. After 2...e6 3. dxe6 fxe6, White loses their central pawn. *[[/2. f4|'''2. f4?!''']], the '''Canard opening'''. *[[/2. Nd2|'''2. Nd2?!''']], hoping to support e4 without preventing c4, should be met with 2...d4, but 2...e4?! is the unsound '''Lazard gambit'''. *[[/2. g4|'''2. g4?!''']], the '''Bronstein gambit''', hopes to tempt Black's knight away from controlling e4 by offering a free flank pawn. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1.d4 Nf6''' {| class="wikitable" |- ! !! 2 !! 3 !! 4 !! 5 !! 6 !! {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Knights variation |parent=
* [[../|Indian defence]] * [[../../../1. Nf3/1...Nf6|Zukertort opening]] |responses=
* [[/2...g6|2...g6 · East Indian defence]] * [[/2...e6|2...e6]] * [[/2...d5|2...d5 · Symmetrical variation]] * [[/2...c5|2...c5 · Spielmann-Indian defence]] * [[/2...d6|2...d6 · Wade-Tartakower defence]] * [[/2...b6|2...b6 · Psuedo-Queen's Indian defence]] }} ==2. Nf3 · Knights variation == This move keeps White's options open: they can first see how Black intends to play before deciding on a response. If, for example, White likes to play against the King's Indian defence with c4, but wants to avoid lines involving c4 and ...e6, they can lead with 2. Nf3 and answer 2...g6 with 3. c4 but 2...e6 with (e.g.) 3. Bg5. This position is also often reached via the move order 1.Nf3 Nf6 2.d4. === Prepare to develop a bishop === Black now makes a decision as to which way they intend to develop their bishop(s). Then, White chooses which line they would like to play, generally from the options 3. c4, 3. g3 (preparing to fianchetto), 3. Bg5 or 3. Bf4, or 3. e3. [[/2...g6|'''2...g6''']] is the most common move. Black prepares to fianchetto their kingside bishop and play in a King's Indian or Grünfeld style. White can transpose into a King's Indian with 3. c4, but other plans include 3. g3, the Przepiorka variation, 3. Bg5, the Torre attack, or 3. Bf4, the London system. [[/2...e6|'''2...e6''']] and Black prepares to deploy their bishop on the a3-f8 diagonal. White has the usual options of 3. c4, 3. g3, 3. Bg5 or 3. Bf4. 3. e3, like the Colle, is called the Yusupov-Rubinstein system. [[/2...b6|'''2...b6''']], the Pseudo-Queens Indian defence, and [[/2...d6|'''2...d6''']], the Wade-Tartakower defence, make a decision about Black's queenside bishop instead. === Play a pawn to the centre === Alternatively, Black can still play a pawn in the centre. If Black plays [[/2...d5|'''2...d5''']] after all, the third most common move, White has the option to transpose into a Queen's gambit. [[/2...c5|'''2...c5''']], the '''Spielmann-Indian''', resembles the Benoni defence (1. d4 c5). White usually pushes the d pawn to d5 save it or defends it with c3 or e3. === Other moves === * [[/2...c6|'''2...c6''']], the '''Czech-Indian''', usually reaches a Slav-style set-up. 3. c4 d5. * [[/2...b5|'''2...b5!?''']], the '''Polish variation''', looks to prevent c4 while preparing ...Bb7. * [[/2...Ne4|'''2...Ne4!?''']] is called the '''Döry defence'''. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Indian defence |parent=[[../|Indian defence]] }} == 2. c4 == White takes more space and increases the control of the important d5 square. This move order allows White's queenside knight to develop to the active c3 square without blocking the c-pawn. Black has a range of different responses and two main plans: contest White's centre immediately with pawns in the classical way, or focus on development and open lines for their bishops, in the [[wikipedia:Hypermodernism (chess)|hypermodern]] way. === Contest the centre with pawns === Capablanca warns us that "two or more pawns are strongest when they are in the same rank next to one another."{{Cite book |title=Chess Fundamentals |last=Capablanca |first=José Raúl |publisher=Harcourt, Brace and Company |year=1921 |location=New York |chapter=6.31. Some salient points about pawns.}} Therefore Black may wish to assault White's pawn centre to force some weaknesses. [[/2...c5|'''2...c5''']] is the '''Benoni defence'''. In theory this is a pawn sacrifice. If White were to play 3. dxc5?!, Black would be very happy to play 3...e6! {{chess/not|=}} (preparing to recapture the pawn; the Weenink variation). Therefore White prefers to keep their d-pawn in the centre with 3. d5. Even though Black cannot remove the d-pawn in this way, at least by forcing it to advance to the next rank, they have weakened the White's grip. After 3. d5 Black tries to attack the pawn chain and play on the queenside. The main continuations are 3...e6, the Modern Benoni (often aggressive, risky), or 3...b5, the Benko gambit (positional pawn sacrifice by Black on the queenside). [[/2...e5|'''2...e5''']] is the '''Budapest defence'''. It has a unique character and often allows Black active play. It offers the e5 pawn with tempo on the knight, 3. dxe5 Ng4, but White usually gives the pawn back eventually. White usually gets a slightly better position, but Black can do well against an unprepared opponent. Black can't transpose into a Queen's gambit declined right now. [[/2...d5|'''2...d5''']] is the '''Marshall defence'''. This allows 3. cxd5 Nxd5 4. e4 Nf6{{Chess/not|+}}, and White gets a big centre and the advantage. === Prepare to develop a bishop === In order to develop their pieces, Black will have to first choose a pawn move to free one of their bishops. Typically the approaches are to free the bishops with ...d6 and ...g6 (what [[wikipedia:Savielly Tartakower|Tartakower]] called "Old Indian defences") or ...e6 and ...b6 (what Tartakower called the "Neo-Indian defences"). [[/2...e6|'''2...e6''']] is the most common move. It is solid and flexible, and prepares to develop the kingside bishop along the a3-f8 diagonal. It also gives Black the option to transpose into a Queen's gambit declined with ...d5. Depending on how White plays and Black responds, this can lead a Queen's Indian defence with ...b6, Nimzo-Indian, Bogo-Indian, Benoni, or a Catalan games. [[/2...b6|'''2...b6''']] is the '''Accelerated Queen's Indian'''. Black prepares to fianchetto their queenside bishop. It is "accelerated" as the Queen's Indian is usually reached through the move order 2...e6 3. Nf3 b6. [[/2...g6|'''2...g6''']], sometimes called the '''West Indian''', prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop. This tends to be a more combative approach. This typically leads to a King's Indian defence, or a Grünfeld after 3. Nc3 d5. [[/2...d6|'''2...d6''']] is called the '''Old Indian'''. This opens the c8-h3 diagonal for the bishop, but Black often develops his knight to d7 first. This can transpose into the King's Indian defence (e.g. 3. Nc3 g6 4. e4 Bg7), but there are lines with their own flavour where Black plays ...e5, ...Be7, and ...O-O. === Other moves === * [[/2...c6|'''2...c6''']] is the rare '''Slav Indian''', looking for a transposition to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6|Slav Defence]]. White typically allows this with 3. Nc3 or 3. Nf3, but can refuse with 3. Bf4. *[[/2...Nc6|'''2...Nc6''']] is the '''Mexican defence''' or '''Black knights tango'''. Though the knight can be kicked immediately with 3. d5, it safely relocates to 3...Ne5. The mainline goes 3. Nf3 (preventing ...e5) e6 4. Nc3 Bb4. *'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...b5|2...b5!?]]''' is a rare response named the '''Pyrenees Gambit''', a dubious wing gambit with the aim of deflecting the c-pawn away from controlling the center. *'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...g5|2...g5?]]''' is a rare, unsound and bad response, gambitting the g5 pawn to 3. Bxg5, named the '''Medusa Gambit'''. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. '''1. d4 Nf6 2. c4'''

pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Indian Defence || }} == 2...e6 == 2...e6 is a move with several purposes. First, it opens a diagonal for the development of Black's dark-squared bishop. It also challenges White's ambition in the center by attacking the d5 square. By doing so, Black prepares to play ...d5 while discouraging White from playing d5 themself. A disadvantage for Black of systems with ...e6 is that the pawn on e6 blocks the c8-h3 diagonal on which Black's light-squared bishop may wish to operate. Finding a useful way to develop this piece, either through a queenside fianchetto or a future reopening of the c8-h3 diagonal, is a perennial challenge for Black players after ...e6. However, the inactivity of the light-squared bishop, while sometimes problematic, is rarely fatal in the early going, and should not discourage Black players from choosing 2...e6 or ...e6 on a later move. White has three main choices here: * [[/3. Nc3/]] - more aggressive in trying to establish a center via e2-e4, but also allows the 3...Bb4 pin (Nimzo-Indian). Black may also play a Benoni (3...c5) or QGD (3...d5). * [[/3. Nf3/]] - Less aggressive but solid. White may face a Queen's Indian (3...b6), Benoni, Bogo-Indian (3...Bb4+), or QGD. * [[/3. g3/]] - This usually leads to a Catalan, or sometimes a Symmetrical English or Benoni. The Catalan offers good chances for White to obtain powerful piece play in a more open game than the typical 1. d4 openings. Less common moves include: * [[/3. Bg5|'''3. Bg5''']], the '''Seirawan attack'''. * [[/3. g4|'''3. g4''']], the '''Devin gambit'''. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}}. '''1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6'''

= Queen's Pawn Opening =

=== 1...Nh6?! ===
This rarer response to 1. d4 plays in a similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nh6|Adams/Hippopotamus Defence]]. Black develops the knight to the rim instead of contesting the center. White can take the center for free or try to ruin Black's pawn structure with Bxh6.

White can choose from a variety of moves, such as:

* 2. c4, playing in the fashion of Queen's Pawn openings
* 2. e4, taking the full center
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight
* 2. Bf4, playing in the fashion of the London
* 2. Bxh6, trading bishop for knight to damage Black's kingside pawn structure.

=== 1...a5?! ===
Black plays in a fashion similar to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...a5|Ware Defence]]. Instead of contesting the center or developing a piece, Black pushes a flank pawn. This rare response to 1. d4 is dubious.

White can choose from a variety of moves, such as:

* 2. e4, taking the full center
* 2. c4, playing in the fashion of Queen's Pawn openings
* 2. Bf4, playing in the fashion of the London
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight

=== 1...a6 ===
This less conventional response to 1. d4 plays in a similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...a6|St. George Defence]], where Black aims to expand on the queenside. Instead of developing a piece or central pawn, Black pushes a flank pawn, but as long as played seriously, this is playable.

White can choose from a variety of moves, such as:

* 2. c4, playing in a normal Queen's Pawn fashion
* 2. Bf4, playing in a London fashion
* 2. e4, transposing to the St. George Defence
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight

__NOTOC__ {{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Old Benoni Defence| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd|nd|rd|= |pd|pd| |pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|= | | | | | | | | |= | | |pd| | | | | |= | | | |pl| | | | |= | | | | | | | | |= |pl|pl|pl| |pl|pl|pl|pl|= |rl|nl|bl|ql|kl|bl|nl|rl|= |moves=1. d4 c5 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A43-A44]] |parent=[[../|Queen's Pawn Opening]] }} == 1...c5 - Old Benoni Defence/ Benoni Defense == The Old Benoni Defense is quite rare and uncommon nowadays but can actually lead to a tactical and sharp game. Black takes a swipe with c5 and gambits a pawn for the exchange, develops, and gets pieces into the game. White normally responds with d5; taking the pawn is not recommended because of 2...e6, and if White tries defending, then a5 and White has no solutions to hold on to pawns while Black gains a tempo. This opening is quite rare nowadays. One idea for Black is to transpose to a Modern Benoni while avoiding the Four Pawn Attack (that is, variations with an early f2-f4 for White). Black can fianchetto his King's Bishop, and only after White plays Nf3 blocking an f-pawn, continue with ... e6 and ... exd5. Another idea for Black is to keep the h8-a1 diagonal of Black's bishop open by delaying ... Nf6. Black could then play ... Ne7 instead of ... Nf6, or possibly, if White plays an early Nc3, give up his bishop by ... Bc3 to double the pawns. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. '''1. d4 c5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Queen's Pawn opening |moves=1.d4 c6 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A40]] |parent=[[../|Queens Pawn Opening]] }} == 1...c6 == {{chess/sideline}} '''1...c6''' is a transpositional tool. Black gives White the option of changing their mind and playing an e4 opening instead. After [[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']], Black can play 2...d5 and transpose into a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6|Slav defence]], as if they had played 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6. With this move order, White has the option of [[/2. e4|'''2. e4''']], where 2...d4 will transpose into a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5|Caro-Kann]], as if they had played 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5. However, if White plays something else, like '''2. Bf4''', going for a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4|Accelerated London]]-style set-up where Black might like to play ...c5 at some point, they may regret having given up a tempo on ...c6 now. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. d4 c6 '''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Position |Closed Game |eco=[[Chess/ECOD|D00-D69]] |parent=[[../|Queen's pawn opening]] |responses=
* [[/2. c4|2. c4 · Queens gambit]] * [[/2. Nf3|2. Nf3 · Zukertort variation]] * [[/2. Bf4|2. Bf4 · Accelerated London system]] * [[/2. Nc3|2. Nc3 · Chigorin variation]] * [[/2. e4|2. e4?! · Blackmar-Diemer gambit]] }} == 1...d5 · Closed game == '''1...d5''' is the classical approach to fighting for the centre: occupying it with pawns. 1...d4 takes some space for Black and opens a line of development for Black's queenside bishop. ===Contest the centre with pawns=== 1...d5 controls the e4 square, so preventing White from securing an ideal two-pawn centre and all the space it would control. White can play [[/2. e4|'''2. e4?!''']] anyway, if they like, but the important thing is they can't keep the pawn there. 2. e4?! is the '''Blackmar-Diemer gambit''', which is considered dubious against best play. After 2...dxe4, White hopes to get a lead in development as compensation for the lost pawn. [[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']], the '''Queen's gambit''', is the mainline. This is a much better try for getting a big centre. White offers the flanking c pawn to Black. Its threat is positional: if Black takes the free pawn, their d-pawn is deflected from its duty controlling the centre. White can then secure a bigger share of the centre for themselves, and should have no trouble recovering the gambitted pawn down the road. Therefore usually Black declines the gambit in one of a number of ways. ===Develop a piece=== Because both colours' d-pawns are already defended by their queens, there is less potential for immediate threats and forcing moves in the Closed game compared to after [[../../1. e4/1...e5|1. e4 e5]]. Therefore, there are a wider range of reasonable turn two options and games have many transpositional possibilities by different move orders. It is usually good to develop a piece when possible, so White may wish to start there. [[/2. Nf3|'''2. Nf3''']] is the '''Zukertort variation'''. This is a flexible move: the knight was almost always going to go to f3, so White plays that move first. White retains the option of playing 3. c4 later (and 2...Nc6 3. c4 is the most common continuation), transposing into a Queen's gambit. Other lines include 3. Bf4, the London system, or 3. e3, the Colle system. 2. Nf3 is the main sideline in tournament play. [[/2. Bf4|'''2. Bf4''']] is the '''Accelerated London system'''. This is the main club-level sideline. It is popular for its straight-forward plans that can be played against a variety of Black move orders. White prioritises developing the bishop so that they can play e3 to support the d-pawn without trapping the bishop behind the pawn chain. White must be conscious of their b2 pawn however, which is now weakened and a source of Black counterplay. [[/2. Nc3|'''2. Nc3''']] is the '''Chigorin variation'''. This is an uncommon move because it prevents White from playing c4. Unlike 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3, here the knight gains no initiative on d5 because the pawn is already protected by Black's queen. After 2...Nf6, the main reply, this can lead to 3. Bg5, the Richter-Veresov attack, or 2. Bf4, the Rapport-Jobava London. === Other sidelines === '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. f4|2. f4]]'''!? is the Mason Attack and is dubious. It controls e5 once more, with the f-pawn. This weakens the kingside and creates a permanent hole on e4. White then usually doubles down with 3. Nf3 and although this is not fully sound, it could be playable. '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. g4|2. g4]]'''? is the Zürich Gambit. It gives up a free pawn to 2...Bxg4 and is very unsound. White usually follows up with Bg2 and Nf3, but the kingside is weakened and the gambit is mostly good with surprise value. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. d4 d5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Queen's pawn opening |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C41]] |parent=[[../|Queen's pawn opening]] }} == 1...d6 == {{chess/sideline}} As with many of Black's off-beat 1st move alternatives, this move does not hold independent status as it usually transposes into other mainstream openings. It is certainly not a bad move on Black's part, but it does allow White to transpose into the Pirc or Modern defence by playing 2. e4, so Black must enjoy playing these defences or should shy from this move. White's options are many. Here are the three most popular: * 2. e4, Pirc or Modern transposition. * 2. c4, allowing 2... e5! Otherwise, heading for various queen's pawn games (e.g. King's Indian defence). * 2. Nf3, keeping the options open while controlling the e5 square. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. d4 d6'''

== 1...e6 · Horwitz defence ==
'''1...e6''' is the Horwitz defence. Black plays something less committal without showing their hand, and waits to see how White wants to approach the game. This can transpose into a myriad of different openings. 

Uniquely, this is an invitation for White to transpose into a '''French defence''' with [[/2. e4|'''2. e4''']]. 

[[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']] is the most common reply, where White keeps the game in Queen's pawn territory. Black can then transpose into a Dutch defence with 2...f5, an Indian defence with 2...Nf6, or a Queen's gambit declined with 2...d5. 2...Bb4+ is known as the Keres or Kangaroo defence. 

Otherwise, White can play almost anything at this point: '''2. Nf3''' and 3. e3 if White is a Colle system player, '''2. Bf4''' should they happen to be a London player, '''2. Nc3''' and 3. Bf4 if they are a Jobava London player, etc, then Black transposes into their preferred line against these moves. 

=== History ===
The Horwitz defence is named for [[Wikipedia:Bernhard Horwitz|Bernhard Horwitz]], a "star" chess player of the group known as the [[wikipedia:Berlin Pleiades|Berlin Pleiades]], who played it several times against [[wikipedia:Daniel Harrwitz|Daniel Harrwitz]] in their 15-game match in Brighton, 1849.<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1044338 Harrwitz - Horwitz (1849) - Chessgames.com]</ref><ref>The existence of the Harrwitz versus Horwitz match implies the existence of further 19th century German chess players Herwitz, Hirwitz, and Hurwitz, but this remains unconfirmed by historians.</ref> 

1...e6 had earlier been tried by Howard Staunton in his 1843 match series against the strongest French player of the time [[wikipedia:Pierre Charles Fournier de Saint-Amant|Saint-Amant]],<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?tid=79243 Staunton - Saint-Amant (1843) - Chessgames.com]</ref> though presumably the world collectively decided that enough things had been named after Staunton by that point. Staunton played it five times, and each game transposed into a Queen's gambit declined with 2. c4 d5. Though 1...e6 didn't bring Staunton much success, he won the match overall and became something of an unofficial World Champion. 

1...e6 is also called the Franco-Indian Defence.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Dutch defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A80-A99]] |parent=[[../|Queen's Pawn Opening]] }} == 1...f5 · Dutch defence == This is the Dutch defence, the fourth most common way to meet 1. d4. Black controls the central e4 square with their flank f-pawn. Because it does not develop or prepare to develop a piece (cf. 1...Nf6 and 1...d5 respectively), 1...f5 is less popular than Black's other options to control e4. In addition, moving the f-pawn so early, before Black has castled, is not for the faint of heart because it weakens Black's kingside. An illustration of this is the classic beginner's trap in the Hopton attack: [[/2. Bg5|2. Bg5]] h6 3. Bh4 g5 3. Bg3 f4 (thinking to trap the bishop) 4. e3 fxg3?? 5. Qh5#. However, the Dutch is very combative, with an original character compared to other 1. d4 openings. Black intends to get maximum value out of a kingside attack. White's main approach against the Dutch is a set-up with Bg2, Nf3, short castling, and c4 by one of a number of move orders. [[/2. g3|'''2. g3''']] is the main move, though [[/2. c4|'''2. c4''']] or [[/2. Nf3|'''2. Nf3''']] are also common and usually transpose. Black chooses between two plans for their kingside bishop: either to fianchetto it with ...g6 and ...Bg7, called the called the '''Leningrad Dutch,''' e.g. 2. c4 Nf6 3. g3 g6 4. Bg2 Bg7; or ...e6 and ...Be7, where they may then choose either ...d6, the '''classical variation''', or an early ...d5 to clamp down on e4, called the '''stonewall variation''', e.g. in the move order 2. c4 Nf6 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. Nf3 O-O 6. O-O d5. If [[/2. e4|'''2. e4?!''']] anyway, the '''Staunton gambit''', Black should be very happy to trade their flank pawn for the more valuable central pawn, 2...fxe5. The Staunton gambit makes sense conceptually―Black has weakened their kingside and slowed down their development, therefore White should open the centre and attack―but while there are many traps available to White involving the weakened e8-h5 diagonal, against best play White is no better than equal. Other sidelines include: [[/2. Bg5|'''2. Bg5''']], the '''Hopton attack'''. If White can't play e4, then they want to ensure the bishop is developed before playing e3. If Black plays 2...Nf6 then White is happy to trade their bishop for it and double Black's pawns. Black can expand on the kingside with tempo against White's bishop, 2...h6 3. Bh4 g5 4. Bg3, so long as they avoid the famous trap (above), or leave the bishop there for now and play 2...g6, ...Bg7 etc. [[/2. Nc3|'''2. Nc3''']], the '''Raphael variation'''. From c3 the knight may help support playing e4 and opening the centre, (e.g. 2...Nf6 (controls e4) 3. Bg5 e6?! 4. e4 fxe4 5. Nxe4{{chess/not|+}}, where 5...h6?? is a rookie error) but usually they games involve Bg5 and e3 as in the Hopton attack, e.g. 2...Nf6 3. Bg5 d5 (to control e4) 4. Bxf6 exf6 5. e3 intending Bd3. [[/2. g4|'''2. g4?!''']], the '''Krejcik gambit''', looks to deflect the f5 pawn from control of e4. However, after 2...fxg4 and ...d5 (defending g4 with the queen's bishop), White will have trouble recapturing the bothersome pawn and find they can't make much of e4 anyway. '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...f5/2. f3|2. f3]]''' is an uncommon sideline aiming for a central push with e4. Sometimes, White gambits a pawn on e4 for quick development and lines. The position is relatively equal after 2...d5 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5=. '''[[/2. Nh3/]]''' is a rare yet sound sideline where White develops the knight to the rim, usually with the intention of the '''Blackburne variation''', after 2...Nf6 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2. '''[[/2. Qd3/]]''', the '''Alapin variation''', aggressively develops the queen and attacks the pawn on f5. === History === Dutch chess master [[w:Elias Stein (chess player)|Elias Stein]] recommended the move 1...f5 in his 1789 ''Nouvel essai sur le jeu des échecs'' (French: ''New essay on the game of chess'') as an alternative to avoid the queen's gambit, 1. d4 d5 2. c4."Celui qui n’a pas le Trait ne veut pas recevoir le Gambit de la Dame.", ''The player without the move (Black) doesn't want to receive the queen's gambit.'' {{Cite book |title=Nouvel essai sur le jeu des échecs |last=Stein |first=Elias |publisher=La Haye |year=1789 |language=French |url=https://archive.org/details/nouvelessaisurl00steigoog/mode/2up |chapter=, Dix-huitieme partie (18th game)}} In the 19th and early 20th centuries, 2. e4?!, the Staunton gambit, was considered critical. In 1931, [[w:Siegbert Tarrasch|Tarrasch]] gave the line 2. e4 fxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 c6 5. f3! exf3, with White being better.{{cite book |title=The Game of Chess |last=Tarrasch |first=Siegbert |year= 1987|orig-year= 1934 |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |isbn= 978-0-486-25447-0}} Though it was never the main line, the Dutch received renewed interest in the 20th century, especially with reappraisal of 2. e4?!. Its most significant outing was in the 1951 World Chess Championship, where it was adopted by [[w:Mikhail Botvinnik|Mikhail Botvinnik]][https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1020397 1951 World Chess Championship, chessgames.com] ==Theory table== '''1. d4 f5''' {| class="wikitable" |- !   !! 2 !! 3 !! 4 !! 5 !! 6 !! 7 !! = Queen's Pawn Opening =

=== 1...f6? ===
A weak response to 1. d4. Playing in similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...f6|Barnes Defence]], Black weakens their king and the e8-h5 diagonal while blocking the kingside knight's most natural square but prepares e5 This is one of the worst responses to 1. d4, only beaten by 1. d4 g5?.

White can choose from a variety of responses, such as:

* 2. e4, taking the full center and poisoning 2...e5
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight and controlling e5.
* 2. c4, playing in the fashion of Queen's Pawn openings.
* 2. Bf4, playing in the fashion of the London and controlling e5
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight

= Queen's Pawn Opening =

=== 1...h5?! ===
Black plays in a similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...h5|Goldsmith Defence]], pushing a flank pawn on the kingside. Instead of contesting the center or developing a piece, Black may want to push their h-pawn to h3 to try and ruin White's kingside. However, this plan is unsound as White grabs the center.

White can choose from a variety of moves, such as:

* 2. e4, taking the full center
* 2. c4, playing in the fashion of Queen's Pawn openings
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight
* 2. Bf4, playing in the fashion of the London
* 2. h4!?, halting the h-pawn's advance

= Queen's Pawn Opening =

=== 1...h6?! ===
A less conventional response to 1. d4, playing in a similar fashion to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...h6|Carr Defence]]. Black wants to gain space on the kingside with g5 and Bg7, however, White can grab the center as Black hasn't contested the center themselves nor developed a piece.

White can choose from a variety of moves, such as:

* 2. e4, taking the full center
* 2. c4, playing in the fashion of Queen's Pawn openings
* 2. Nf3, developing the kingside knight
* 2. Nc3, developing the queenside knight
* 2. Bf4, playing in the fashion of the London, but the bishop can be kicked with 2...g5
* 2. h4!?, stopping g5.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Van 't Kruijs opening |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A00]] |parent=[[../|Starting position]] }} == 1. e3 · Van 't Kruijs Opening == An irregular opening, considered somewhat passive, as although White opens lines for their bishop and queen to enter the game, Black is given the opportunity to take over the centre with ...e5 and ...d5. Black may play any number of moves to stake a claim in the centre: [[/1...Nf6|'''1...Nf6''']], [[/1...e5|'''1...e5''']], [[/1...d5|'''1...d5''']], [[/1...c5|'''1...c5''']] are all reasonable. [[/1...g6|'''1...g6''']], intending ...Bg7, or 1...Nf6 followed by 2...g6, is a typical approach to meet lots of transpositions equally. Many openings for White feature e3 at some point, so play can transpose into lines of the [[Chess/English Opening|English Opening]] if White plays c4, [[Chess/Queen's Pawn Opening|Queen's Pawn Opening]] with d4, [[Chess/Larsen's Opening|Larsen's Opening]] with b3 and Bb2, and so on. A consideration is that the pawn on e3 prevents development of White's queenside bishop: White must concede a tempo with e4, passively develop it to d2, or fianchetto it to b2. Uniquely, play can proceed with 1...e5 2. e4!?, which arrives at an Open Game (1. e4 e5) but with colours reversed, where it is Black's turn to move. After 1...Nf6 2. Nf3 g6 3. b4 Bg7 4. Bb2 O-O 5. c4 d6 6. d4, the most common continuation, play reaches a King's Indian-type position. == Theory table == {{clear}} {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e3'''
